text: A wheel of magnets.
No fuel. No plug.
It never stops.
Twelve sixty-nine. A French army besieges Lucera, in Italy.
One of its engineers, Peter Peregrinus, writes a letter about magnets.
In it: a wheel that magnets would drive around forever.
In the sixteen hundreds, English scholar John Wilkins describes a ramp.
A magnet at the top pulls an iron ball up.
It drops through a hole, rolls back down, and climbs again.
Seventeen seventy-five. The Paris Academy of Sciences
says it will no longer deal with perpetual motion.
Today, the U.S. patent office can demand a working model.
So why does every magnet wheel stop?
A magnet's pull is a hill.
Every bit of help going in is paid back coming out.
Over one full turn, the sum is zero.
Friction takes the rest, and the wheel parks at its sticky point.
Lodestone asks: what if the sticky point could be switched off?
Twenty-four magnets on a one point two meter rotor.
Trial one. Bare magnets.
Three turns. Stopped.
Trial two. A shield slides over the sticky point.
Eleven turns. Stopped. Moving the shield costs what it saves.
Trial three. A coil fires at the sticky point and cancels the pull.
Forty days. Still turning.
One catch.
The coil runs on a battery.
Lodestone is cleared.
As an electric motor.
Peregrinus wanted a wheel that never stops.
We built one. It has a plug.
